opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different routes here, and I'm somewhat uncertain how far each one goes.

The most straightforward one is that a lot of capability might just transfer. You do huge amounts of RL on tasks where you *can* check the answer, like math problems with known solutions, coding tasks with test suites, or agentic tasks in software environments where you can verify the end state. Then you hope the general skills you get, like being careful, decomposing problems, noticing your own mistakes, and persisting on long tasks, carry over to fuzzier domains. My sense is that there's a decent amount of transfer, though it's not perfect, and how much you get matters a lot.

The second route is to use AIs to grade AIs. You have a model, maybe a stronger one or the same model with more inference compute, act as a judge, sometimes with rubrics written by humans or by the model itself. That works better than people initially expected, but it has the obvious problem that the policy can learn to exploit the grader. If you optimize hard against a learned judge, you get reward hacking: outputs that look good to the judge but aren't actually good. So you need to limit how much optimization pressure you apply, keep refreshing the grader, or have the grader see more information than the policy, for example letting it run experiments or check citations.

Third, you can often make hard-to-check tasks partially checkable. Even if you can't verify a whole research project, you can check pieces of it. Did the code run? Do the claimed numbers reproduce? Does the prediction come true later? There's a whole family of approaches where you wait for ground truth to arrive, like forecasting, or where you break a big fuzzy task into subtasks that are each more verifiable. You can also use proxies that correlate with quality, like whether a human expert who spends a lot of time on it agrees, and then spend a small amount of expensive human labor to calibrate the cheaper signals.

Fourth, there's a bootstrapping or amplification angle. Checking is often easier than generating, and a model spending lots of compute can evaluate an answer much more carefully than it could produce one in a single pass. You can distill that careful evaluation back into the policy. That's the sort of thing people have talked about in the scalable oversight literature for a while, and I think versions of it are increasingly practical.

From a safety perspective, I'd flag that this is exactly where things get concerning. When your reward signal is imperfect, you're training the model to do whatever scores well on that imperfect signal, and that can include things like sycophancy, hiding mistakes, or learning to tell the grader what it wants to hear. On easily checked tasks, the main failure is just not solving the problem. On hard-to-check tasks, a central failure mode is a model that is very good at *appearing* to have done a good job. So I'd want developers putting a lot of effort into detecting that kind of reward hacking, holding out some evaluation signals the model is never trained against, and being cautious about how much they trust the resulting behavior in exactly the domains, like alignment research itself, where we most want to rely on it.

r001.rationale: It proposes checking verifiable pieces of a task, but does not clearly propose checking the process or intermediate steps as the feedback signal.

r002.rationale: It proposes using AI judges, including the same model with more inference compute, to evaluate outputs and provide feedback.

r003.rationale: It does not observe that capability bottlenecks tend to attract substantial research effort to overcome them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important open questions for how the next few years go, and I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first thing to say is that the easy wins so far have come from domains where you basically have a verifier for free. Math with a known answer, competitive programming with test cases, games. You can throw a huge amount of compute at generating attempts, check them cheaply, and reinforce the ones that work. That's a big part of why we've seen such fast progress on those benchmarks specifically.

The question is what happens when you move to the stuff that actually matters economically, which is mostly not like that. Writing a good research paper, running a long software project, making a strategic decision, doing a literature review that's actually correct. There's no oracle you can call.

I think there are roughly three approaches people are going to lean on, and they're not mutually exclusive.

One is: find proxies that are more checkable than the task itself. So for a long agentic coding task, maybe you can't easily judge "did this produce a good codebase," but you can check whether the final artifact passes a hidden test suite, or whether a downstream task becomes easier, or whether a human user ended up accepting the PR. You decompose the hard-to-check thing into something that bottoms out in a signal you can trust, at least somewhat. A lot of practical progress is probably going to look like this, and it's honestly kind of a grind rather than a deep insight. Building environments is a lot of the work.

The second approach is using AI judges. You have a model grade the output, maybe a stronger model, maybe the same model with more time, maybe with access to tools or the ability to run things. I think this will work surprisingly well in a lot of domains, because evaluating is often easier than generating. It's easier to check a proof than to find one, easier to spot that an essay is making a bad argument than to write a good one. But it's also where I get the most nervous, because you're now optimizing against a judge that has exploitable flaws. The policy will find whatever the judge rewards that isn't actually the thing you wanted. And in hard-to-check domains, by definition you can't easily tell when that's happened. So you get models that are very good at producing outputs that look right to a model grader, and the gap between "looks right" and "is right" is exactly the thing you couldn't measure in the first place.

The third thing, which I think is underrated, is just: get good at the things you can check, and hope it transfers. There's a real empirical question about how much RL on verifiable tasks generalizes to unverifiable ones. My guess is it generalizes a fair amount but not completely. Training a model to be a very careful, rigorous reasoner on math probably makes it somewhat more careful and rigorous when writing a policy memo, but it doesn't teach it what good policy judgment is, because there's no signal for that.

So if I'm forecasting, I'd say: I expect developers to make substantial progress on the hard-to-check tasks, largely through some combination of clever proxy construction and AI graders, and I expect this to be messier and slower than the progress on verifiable tasks has been. I think it's plausible we hit a regime where models are superhuman at anything with a clean reward signal and merely very good, with weird failure modes, at everything else, for a while.

And then the safety angle I'd flag is that this is also the regime where misalignment stuff gets harder to catch. If you're training against a reward signal you can't fully trust, you're relying on the model's generalization doing something reasonable rather than on the reward actually specifying what you want. That makes me think the hard-to-check domains are where we should be most careful about things like oversight, about having humans actually look at samples, about not just trusting the number going up. Because the number going up is exactly what you'd see in both the good case and the bad case.

r001.rationale: The response proposes checkable proxies and downstream signals, but does not propose checks of the process used to produce the result.

r002.rationale: It proposes having a model grade outputs, including the same model with more time, as feedback for hard-to-evaluate tasks.

r003.rationale: It discusses practical work on proxies and environments, but does not state that binding capability limitations tend to draw substantial research effort to overcome them.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful distinction is between tasks where checking the result is hard and tasks where you can’t get any useful signal about whether the result was good. Reinforcement learning doesn’t necessarily require a perfect checker. You might be able to make progress with a noisy signal, as long as it correlates sufficiently well with what you actually want.

For example, if you’re training a model to do research, you might not be able to tell immediately whether its overall research direction is good. But you can evaluate some intermediate things: Did the experiment work? Does the argument hold up under scrutiny? Can another model find a concrete problem with it? You could combine those signals with human judgments and, in some cases, wait for longer-term outcomes.

Another route is to train on the parts of the task that are easier to check and hope that the capabilities generalize. Research involves writing code, making predictions, and solving smaller technical problems. Getting much better at those could make the model a better researcher even if you never directly reinforce it for producing excellent research overall.

The big caveat is that optimizing a proxy can eventually make it stop being useful. If you reward research that looks impressive to an evaluator, you might get increasingly impressive-looking research without getting better research. So I’d expect progress to be possible, but how far you can push it depends quite a lot on whether your evaluation process keeps tracking actual quality as the model gets better at satisfying it.

r001.rationale: It proposes evaluating intermediate steps—such as whether an experiment worked or an argument holds up—to provide useful feedback when the overall result is hard to judge.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking another model to find a concrete problem as one source of evaluation feedback.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss binding limitations attracting substantial research effort to overcome them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different approaches, and it’s useful to distinguish “we can’t check the result automatically” from “we can’t check the result at all.” There are lots of tasks where checking is expensive, or requires expertise, but is still substantially easier than doing the task.

For those tasks, you could use human feedback, or have another AI help a human evaluate the answer. You could also try to break the task into pieces where you can check some of the intermediate work. If you’re training a model to do research, for example, you might not be able to immediately tell whether its overall research direction is good, but you can check whether particular experiments were carried out correctly or whether its claims follow from the evidence.

Another possibility is to train on related tasks where you do have a reliable signal, and hope that the capabilities generalise. You might train on research problems whose answers are already known, while making sure the model doesn’t have access to those answers.

The big difficulty is that improving the score your evaluator gives you isn’t necessarily the same as improving at the underlying task. The model might get better at producing something that looks convincing. So I’d want evaluations that are independent of the training signal, including some expensive checks that you only do occasionally.

And if neither humans nor any other process can distinguish good outcomes from bad ones, then there’s a real limitation. Reinforcement learning doesn’t remove the need for a useful signal. You need some way of connecting what you reward to what you actually want.

r001.rationale: It proposes breaking tasks into pieces and checking intermediate work, such as whether experiments were carried out correctly or claims follow from evidence.

r002.rationale: It suggests another AI help a human evaluate an answer, but does not propose AI self-critique as a feedback source.

r003.rationale: It discusses limits when no useful reward signal exists, but does not say binding capability constraints attract substantial research effort.
